today.description: Let your agents use 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps, from Salesforce to GitHub, through one MCP gateway. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

We treat measurement as step one, not the product. The product is the movement from unmentioned, to cited, to recommended. ReSO is your company’s employee who takes ownership of results.Who its for: Founders, SEO & content teams, and agencies who can see search shifting and want a system & not another report to win it.🎁 For the PH community: Free AI visibility audit of your brand & 100% off one month access for launch-week signups worth USD 599🙏 Our ask: Honest feedback over upvotes. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
